I study how climate shapes the growth, function, and survival of trees — from the
slow pressure of shifting averages to the sharp blows of drought and heat, and
the long shadow these leave behind. My work combines **ecological and climate
time-series analysis**, **statistical and machine-learning models**, and
**dynamical-systems thinking**, drawing on dendrometer records, flux-tower data,
global tree-ring archives, and high-resolution climate datasets.

Across projects, a single question recurs: *how does a changing climate reshape
the long-term trajectory of tree growth, function, and survival?* I approach it
from several directions at once — data-driven, mechanistic, and instrumental —
because the answer lives at the intersection of all three.

---

## Which way is forest growth headed?

Under climate change, will forests grow more or less? The honest answer is that
it depends on where you look — and those local differences have tended to cancel
out into a shrug, hiding whether there is any overall direction at all.

I ask whether that direction can be recovered. The approach is to let the data
define the climate–growth relationship rather than assume it: I learn the
**nonlinear response of tree growth to temperature, precipitation, and
atmospheric water demand** from thousands of tree-ring records across the
Northern Hemisphere, then push those relationships forward under climate
projections to see where each forest lands. Reading the results not as a single
snapshot but as trajectories through time turns out to matter — it separates
losses that stick from gains that quietly fade.

## Can the tree-ring record speak for a changing climate? {.ongoing}

Almost everything we know about tree growth at large scales rests on one archive:
the global network of tree-ring records. But that archive was never assembled to
be representative — it was built site by site, often chasing strong climate
signals in cold or dry places. So a natural question is *what climates it can
actually speak for.*

I am building a **climate-space audit** of the archive: placing forests and the
sampled records in a shared, multi-season climate space and asking how much of
the climate that forests live in today — and will live in tomorrow — sits close
to something we have actually measured. Two distinctions drive it: being *near* a
sampled climate is not the same as being *well supported* by many of them; and a
sampling bias that looks like a weakness today may, by chance, point in the same
direction the climate is moving — pre-positioning the record for some future
forests while leaving others increasingly off the map. The aim is a clear picture
of where tree-ring–based inference stands on solid ground, and where new sampling
would help most.

---

## When do survivable droughts become lethal in sequence? {.ongoing}

Tree death from drought is usually weighed one event at a time — how hot, how dry,
how long. But trees live through *sequences* of droughts, and a drought that is
survivable on its own can leave lasting marks: depleted carbon reserves, hydraulic
damage, a thinned canopy. The next drought then arrives at a tree that is no longer
the same tree.

I am developing a deliberately **minimal dynamical-systems model** of a tree's
carbon and hydraulic state to explore this memory. The question is not "how severe
was the drought" but *when does history tip the balance* — when do successive
events buffer one another, when do they compound, and when does incomplete recovery
carry a tree past the point of return.

The picture below is the intuition behind the model. Imagine a plane whose axes are
the tree's water status and its carbon reserves. A healthy, self-restoring state
sits in one corner, separated by a threshold — a *line of no return* — from states
that slide toward death. A drought bends the flow and pushes the tree off its
healthy state; when it passes, recovery begins, but *from wherever the tree was
left*. A second drought that full health would have shrugged off can, if it lands
before recovery is complete, carry the tree across that line. History, not just
total severity, decides the outcome.

## Reading drought from the stem, hour by hour

Drought reaches a tree two ways at once — through the **soil**, as water runs
short at the roots, and through the **atmosphere**, as dry air pulls water from
the canopy. They usually arrive together, which makes their separate fingerprints
hard to tell apart.

I use trees' own micro-movements to pull them apart. High-resolution
**dendrometers** record a stem swelling and shrinking through the day, and pairing
them with an irrigation experiment — where relieving soil drought leaves only the
atmospheric signal — lets me read growth, water status, and recovery straight from
the stem. It shows, among other things, that whether a heatwave merely slows a tree
or tips it into shrinking depends on the soil water it has to fall back on.

## Future directions

My longer-term interest is the **mechanistic basis of tree growth and mortality
under climate change** — how the twin currencies of tree health, **carbon** and
**water**, are drawn down as the climate shifts, and how that decides which trees
recover and which cross the line into decline.

I want to keep working across scales and methods: from **individual-tree
physiology** measured at high resolution, to **continental patterns** in the
tree-ring record, to **mechanistic models** that tie the two together — and, where
it helps, building the **sensors** that gather the data in the first place. The
unifying goal is to understand, and eventually forecast, forest **resilience and
vulnerability**: not just how trees respond to the climate they have known, but how
they will fare in the climates they are about to meet.

I am **seeking postdoc opportunities beginning fall 2027**, and I welcome
conversations about projects and collaborations along these lines.
